home.whySubtitle: Digital transparency for an informed citizenry
home.mission: In times where access to public information is increasingly difficult, we believe that monitoring the government's digital infrastructure is an act of civic transparency. Government websites are the gateway to public services, procedures, and official data. When these sites fail or become inaccessible, citizens lose access to fundamental rights.

methodology.title: How we measure
methodology.frequencyText: Every 6 hours an automated monitor visits each of the 2,500+ domains (HTTPS, falling back to HTTP), with a second pass for the ones that did not respond. Every result is stored: the history grows with each check.
methodology.vantageText: Checks go out through an IP that geolocation databases place in Caracas, Venezuela (a VPN server physically in Miami). This avoids country-based blocking, but it does not measure the experience of a user on a Venezuelan network.
methodology.qualityText: If the number of active sites in a check drops below half of the usual, the problem is our connection, not the sites: that check is discarded and does not appear in charts or history.
methodology.archiveText: Every day we send a copy of every active site to the Internet Archive, starting with those never archived and those that just changed, so a record remains if a site disappears. Sites that are down are not sent.
methodology.estimatesText: Level of government, state and sector are inferred from the domain name, because WHOIS does not identify the agency in most cases. They are approximations.
